title: Be Proud Of This
author: The Daily Dad
summary: Drawing on The Girl Who Would Be Free, a children's fable based on the Stoic philosopher Epictetus, this Daily Dad piece argues that a parent's dignity comes from how they do their work, not from its status or pay. The fable's father, stuck at the bottom of Rome's social hierarchy digging sewage canals, teaches his daughter that they cannot choose their circumstances but can choose not to add to their troubles by complaining, and that doing any job well, no matter how humble, can be beautiful. The piece extends this directly to modern fatherhood, arguing a single parent working long restaurant shifts is more genuinely impressive than a 'half-assing stockbroker,' since true philosophy lies in focusing on what's in one's control and doing the work seriously rather than in job titles or market compensation. It closes by explicitly telling readers that showing up and doing what needs to be done for their family already earns them the right to feel proud.
points: The fable's central Stoic move is refusing to let circumstance define dignity: the father tells his daughter 'we didn't choose this, but we can choose not to add to our troubles by complaining about them.'
His maxim 'how you do anything is how you do everything' reframes even degrading, low-status labor (digging sewage canals) as an opportunity for the same excellence available to any job.

The piece makes an explicit economic inversion: 'the single parent working long shifts in a restaurant is far more impressive than the half-assing stockbroker anyway, even if the market compensates these two roles very differently.'

It closes by directly telling readers doing right by their family is sufficient grounds for self-respect regardless of job title: 'you are taking care of your family. You are doing what needs to be done. That's enough to earn you the respect of yourself, and the people who matter.'
quotes: We didn't choose this," he tells his daughter, "but we can choose not to add to our troubles by complaining about them.
How you do anything is how you do everything. And if you do it well, it can be beautiful, no matter what it is.
No one has the power to degrade us," he says, "only themselves by being unfair and unkind.
The single parent working long shifts in a restaurant is far more impressive than the half-assing stockbroker anyway, even if the market compensates these two roles very differently.
Epictetus taught his students that freedom lies in wanting only what we can control: our character, our choices, our reasoned response.
You are taking care of your family. You are doing what needs to be done. That's enough to earn you the respect of yourself, and the people who matter.
